abstract.p: Neuropeptides mediate inter-tissue communication in energy metabolism, yet most remain functionally uncharacterized. Using C. elegans, we uncover a neuropeptide signaling cascade that drives lipid catabolism under chronic dietary restriction. We show that impaired pharyngeal function leads to dyspepsia and nutrient insufficiency, which activates a signaling axis comprising two peptide-receptor pairs, NLP-10-NPR-35 and FLP-18-NPR-4. This cascade originates in ADL sensory neurons, relays through multiple interneurons, and enhances triglyceride hydrolysis in the intestine. Genetic disruption of any component of this axis restores fat accumulation in diet-restricted mutants, whereas overexpression of individual components in well-fed animals is insufficient to drive fat mobilization. Importantly, the same neuropeptide axis is engaged in starved wild-type animals, indicating a general response toward energy deficit rather than mutant-specific effects. These findings reveal a conserved neuroendocrine circuit that senses internal energy shortage and orchestrates systemic metabolic adaptation, providing a conceptual framework for how neuropeptide networks integrate nutritional status with energy balance in animals.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Energy metabolism is orchestrated by multi-tissue neuroendocrine networks in animals. Acting as messengers between the central nervous system and peripheral metabolic tissues, neuropeptides play key regulatory roles in this process, coupling nutrient availability to physiological responses that govern the storage or mobilization of neutral lipids. In mammals, hypothalamic and brainstem circuits integrate peripheral hormonal cues (e.g., insulin, leptin) with central neuropeptidergic signals (e.g., AgRP, α-MSH) to regulate adiposity and appetite1,2. Despite well-defined examples, the vast majority of neuropeptide systems remain functionally uncharacterized. In humans, although 462 neuropeptide-receptor pairs involving 225 neuropeptides have been predicted3, most have no characterized functions 4. This gap is further complicated by ligand-receptor redundancy and the often-dominant effects of hormones, which can obscure the subtle yet critical contributions of specific neuropeptide pathways to energy homeostasis5–7.

The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans)8 provides a powerful platform to dissect neuropeptide functions, given its evolutionarily conserved metabolic pathways9, genetically tractable neuropeptide connectomes10,11, and direct peptide-receptor communication via pseudocoelom8. A previous genetic screen revealed that mutants lacking functional Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) signaling exhibit significant fat loss in intestine12, a phenotype confirmed in this study and by other publications13,14. Metabolic tracing demonstrated that the BMP-associated fat loss arises from accelerated lipid mobilization (e.g., mitochondrial β oxidation of fatty acids), rather than reduced fat synthesis12. The BMP signaling pathway is a branch of the TGF-β superfamily (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)15–18; however, the mechanistic link between BMP deficiency and peripheral fat loss has remained elusive.

Notably, genetic restoration of BMP signaling in the pharynx fully rescued the intestinal fat accumulation12, exhibiting a cell-non-autonomous working pattern. Given that pharyngeal muscles of wildtype C. elegans provide food grinding forces to crush bacterial food19, and dbl-1 mutants had more intestinal bacteria under normal feeding conditions20,21, we hypothesize that pharyngeal BMP signaling regulates food grinding to control intestinal fat storage via inter-tissue mechanisms. Long distance diffusion of neuropeptides allows inter-tissue communication22–24, serving as ideal candidates to mediate cell-non-autonomous responses.

Here, we uncovered that the BMP-associated fat loss is caused by pharyngeal impairments and subsequently insufficient food grinding, and the pharynx-to-intestine regulation relies on a hierarchy neuropeptide signaling axis. In this axis, the ADL sensory neurons release neuropeptide NLP-10 to activate its receptor NPR-35, which functions in interneurons to promote the secretion of a lipid-regulating neuropeptide, FLP-18. Abundant FLP-18 stimulates the intestinal receptor NPR-4 to promote fat loss, a process requiring adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL-1) and other lipases. Importantly, this neuropeptide axis is not merely a mutant-specific phenomenon: In fasted wild-type animals, the same NLP-10/NPR-35 and FLP-18/NPR-4 modules are engaged to promote lipid catabolism, suggesting a general, conserved neural mechanism for fat mobilization in response to nutrient deprivation. Our findings establish neuropeptides as systemic neuroendocrine hubs that link nutrient processing to organism-wide metabolic adaptation, thereby synchronizing animal physiology with nutrient availability.

sec.title: BMP mutants are dyspeptic and chronically diet-restricted
sec.p: Consistent with previous findings12, suppression of DBL-1 or SMA-6 was sufficient to reduce the intestinal fat contents in C. elegans (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). By scoring colony-forming units (CFU) within the C. elegans gastrointestinal tract, and by measuring relative fluorescent intensity of the GFP-positive bacterial food (OP50-GFP) within C. elegans’ gastrointestinal tract, we affirmed that the BMP mutants contained more viable bacteria (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). Observation of intestinal cross-sections by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed frequent bacterial presence in the gastrointestinal lumen of the BMP mutants, but not in wildtype (Figure 1C, Figure 1— figure supplement 1D).

sec.p: Pharyngeal muscles of wildtype C. elegans are fulfilled with myofilaments aligned at angles approximately perpendicular to the anterior-posterior body axis25. Indeed, cross-section TEM images of wildtype pharynx showed long and continuous myofilaments accompanied by healthy mitochondria; In contrast, myofilaments of sma-6(wk7) are short, gapped, and chaotically aligned, accompanied by pale mitochondria (Figure 1D). Above findings suggest that lacking BMP pathway has impaired the pharyngeal muscle, which could very likely reduce the pharyngeal food grinding force. Consistently, previous findings confirmed the requirement of pharyngeal BMPs in regulating intestinal fat storage26. Simultaneously, we detected bacterial lysate (similar to the lysate of ultrasound-treated E. coli27) in the gastrointestinal lumens of both wildtype and BMP mutants (Figure 1C). Although we did not distinguish whether bacterial death occurred prior to ingestion or resulted from pharyngeal grinding, we think that the BMP mutants could derive at least some nutrients (if not sufficient amounts) from their routine laboratory diet.

If nutrient deficiency was the reason behind BMP-associated fat loss, then we would expect the BMP mutants to benefit from absorbing edible nutrients for fat accumulation. We respectively supplemented wildtype or sma-6(wk7) with small molecule nutrients – either glucose, fructose or oleic acid (OA) – in addition to the routine bacterial diet. All three types of nutrients restored the intestinal fat levels in sma-6(wk7) at relatively low doses that would not disturb wildtype fat contents (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F). Such nutrient-dependent fat restoration likely occurred via metabolic pathways downstream of or independent from the defective BMP signaling, demonstrating that the BMP mutants are viable and fertile animal models with consistent dyspepsia and chronical dietary restriction.

sec.title: Neuropeptide signaling promotes lipid catabolism in sma-6 mutants
sec.p: By analyzing the relative gene expression levels of sma-2(rax5) versus wildtype, and sma-4(rax10) versus wildtype12, we predicted differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Then we utilized Gene Ontology (GO) analysis on the intersection of genes induced in both sma-2(rax5) and sma-4(rax10), and the neuropeptide signaling pathway was highlighted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Given that the secretion of neuropeptides require dense core vesicles (DSVs), we disrupted unc-31, which encodes the conserved Ca2+-dependent activator protein for secretion (CAPS) to mediate DSV docking and priming in C. elegans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)28–30. Disruption of unc-31 facilitated intestinal fat accumulation in BMP mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), confirming the involvement of neuropeptide secretion in regulating BMP-associated fat loss.

To address the specific neuropeptides in regulating fat mobilization, we verify the RNA-seq results by qRT-PCR on total mRNA samples from young adults of wildtype, sma-6(wk7), dbl-1(wk70) and sma-2(rax5), with primers respectively targeting neuropeptide-encoding genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, supplementary Table 1). Besides, we compared our qRT-PCR results (rectangles) to the 16h-fasted gene expression data in Harvald et al31 (ovals). Indeed, a majority of neuropeptide genes exhibited upregulation in both datasets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

Next, we obtained either a loss-of-function mutant or a feeding-based RNAi strain for 41 of 73 neuropeptide genes. For each, we generated double knockdowns of a neuropeptide gene and a BMP gene. Then we compared the intestinal fat levels of the double knockdowns to their corresponding siblings with functional neuropeptides but dysfunctional BMP signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, supplementary Table 2). Among all genes required in the BMP-associated fat loss, despite that some neuropeptides were known to regulate lipid metabolism under other contexts (e.g., flp-1824,32 and nlp-1233), the evolutionarily conserved nlp-10 attracted our attention, as it was consistently upregulated in different types of BMP mutants and starved animals, and also capable to suppress fat accumulation in the BMP mutants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F). Furthermore, we generated transgenic strains overexpressing nlp-10 by an endogenous promoter or a pan-neural promoter in sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232), and these transgenic animals failed to accumulate sufficient fat, phenocopying the low-fat status of sma-6(wk7) (Figure 2B, C).

sec.title: BMP-associated fat loss is regulated by NLP-10 secreted from ADL neurons
sec.p: Based on C. elegans gene expression databases including WormSeq34, CeNGEN35, CAWA36, and CaenoGen37, as well as the DiI-based imaging on the transcriptional reporter nlp-10p::GFP, we confirmed that nlp-10 mainly expresses in neurons, including amphid neurons ADL (Figure 3A). In sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232) with ADL-specific expression of nlp-10, the fat levels were as low as that of sma-6(wk7) (Figure 3B). Consistently, genetic ablation of ADL neurons in sma-6(wk7), achieved by two independent ADL-specific TeTx (light chain of tetrodotoxin) lines38, enabled fat restoration in sma-6(wk7) (Figure 3C), resembling the nlp-10 suppression in BMP mutants.

sec.p: The pharyngeal rescue of SMA-3 by the myo-2p::SMA-3 transgene has been shown to restore the low-fat phenotype of sma-3(wk30) 26, and ADL neurons are known to express sma-6 in addition to its nlp-10 expression34,35. So, we wondered if sma-6 might have worked in the ADL neurons to transcriptionally regulate nlp-10, and we specifically restored the expression of SMA-6 in the ADL neurons of sma-6(wk7). Yet the fat levels remained low in these transgenic worms (Figure 3D), suggesting that sma-6 does not work in the ADL neurons to regulate fat contents. Together, we hypothesize a model that the BMP deficiency has impaired pharyngeal food grinding to generate chronical dietary-restriction at individual level, and such diet-restricted status would trigger the ADL neurons to release NLP-10 to remotely facilitate lipid catabolism in intestine (Figure 3E). In BMP mutants, given that suppressing other peptides was also sufficient to alleviate fat loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), NLP-10 is unlikely to be the exclusive peptide with lipid regulatory roles. Yet it serves as a good entry point for us to further investigate the downstream mechanisms, as it is robustly upregulated in all examined BMP mutants, and also has a known receptor, NPR-3511,39. Based on these findings, we sought to focus on how NLP-10 mediates lipid catabolism.

sec.title: NPR-35 functions in interneurons to promote BMP-associated fat loss
sec.p: To our knowledge, npr-35 encodes the sole known receptor of NLP-1011,39–42. Fat levels of sma-6(wk7); npr-35(ok3258) were greater than that of sma-6(wk7), resembling sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232); However, the triple mutant sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232); npr-35(ok3258) accumulated even more fat than that of sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232) or sma-6(wk7); npr-35(ok3258) (Figure 4A), indicating involvement of unknown ligands for npr-35 or unknown receptors for nlp-10, or both.

sec.p: The npr-35-expressing tissues mainly covers interneurons34,35,43, including AIY, AVA, AVD, AVE, etc. In sma-6(wk7); npr-35(ok3258), we performed AVA, AVD, AVE, RIM, SIB-specific rescue of npr-35 with nmr-1 promoter (Figure 4B), and AIY-specific rescue of npr-35 with ttx-3 promoter (Figure 4C), and fat levels of sma-6(wk7); npr-35(ok3258) were suppressed by either transgene, supporting ectopic regulation of NPR-35 on BMP-associated fat deficiency. Interestingly, removal of npr-35 failed to offset the fat deficiency in sma-6(wk7); Ex[nlp-10p::NLP-10] (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), further suggesting that one or more unrevealed NLP-10 receptors could be required in regulating BMP-associated fat loss. Meanwhile, the neuronal but not gastrointestinal function of NPR-35 indicates that downstream mechanisms, which should signal from interneurons to intestine, are required to regulate BMP-associated fat loss.

sec.title: npr-35-expressing neurons release FLP-18 to mediate fat mobilization in BMP mutants
sec.p: Interestingly, a large proportion of npr-35-expressing neurons also express flp-18 (Figure 4D), a peptide that is required for the BMP-associated fat loss in our initial screens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E). This expressive intersection has included AIY, AVA, AVD and other aforementioned interneurons34,35. So, we went on to investigate links between NLP-10, NPR-35 and FLP-18.

To verify if the npr-35-expressing neurons would alter fat contents via FLP-18, we compared the fat levels of sma-6(wk7); flp-18(tm2179) strains with or without the npr-35p::FLP-18 transgene, and it turns out that the fat contents of sma-6(wk7); flp-18(tm2179); Ex[npr-35p::FLP-18] was as low as that of sma-6(wk7) (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). Besides, expression of flp-18 in the AIY neurons achieved by the ttx-3p::FLP-18 transgene in sma-6(wk7); flp-18(tm2179) could restore fat levels to be sma-6(wk7)-like (Figure 4F). Together, we conclude that flp-18 was required in npr-35-expressing interneurons for the sma-6(wk7) animals to mobilize fat.

sec.title: Downstream of FLP-18, intestinal NPR-4 mediates BMP-associated fat loss
sec.p: As a known receptor of FLP-18, NPR-4 regulates intestinal fat storage in other contexts24,32. A transcriptional reporter of npr-4p::GFP confirmed its neuronal and intestinal expression (Figure 5A), and knockout of npr-4 in BMP mutants led to restored fat accumulation (Figure 5B). Genetic rescue of npr-4 by its endogenous promoter (Figure 5C) or the intestinal-specific promoter ges-1p (Figure 5D, Figure 5— figure supplement 1A) could suppress fat accumulation in sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782), supporting an in-situ lipid regulatory role of NPR-4 in BMP mutants.

sec.p: Notably, sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782) contained more fat than that of sma-6(wk7); flp-18(tm2179) (Figure 5B), indicating ligand redundancy. We tested other known ligands of NPR-439,40, and we found that FLP-4 and FLP-1 were also required to mediate BMP-associated fat loss (Figure 5E-F), whereas FLP-14 and FLP-21 were dispensable (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C). Unlike FLP-18, which is co-expressed with NPR-35, FLP-1 has very limited expressive overlap with this receptor34,35, and our data demonstrate that FLP-1 does not seem to be secreted from the npr-35-expressing neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

To test if npr-4 deletion was sufficient to block the BMP-associated fat loss mediated by FLP-18, we directly compared the fat levels of sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782); Ex[ttx-3p::FLP-18] with sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782) and sma-6(wk7); Ex[ttx-3p::FLP-18]. Regardless of FLP-18 overexpression, sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782) contained equivalently abundant amount of fat (Figure 5G), suggesting that npr-4 works downstream of flp-18. On the other hand, overexpression of the upstream neuropeptide NLP-10 cannot alter the fat levels of sma-6(wk7); npr-4(tm1782), either (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). These results imply a regulatory axis consisted of NLP-10-to-NPR-35, FLP-18-to-NPR-4 in the upstream-to-downstream order, with FLP-1 and FLP-4 being additively required in parallel to FLP-18.

sec.title: Fat breakdown in BMP mutants requires lipolysis
sec.p: By lipidomic analysis, in sma-6(wk7) we found that a majority of triglycerides (TG) were reduced, and almost all diglycerides (DG) were increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, supplementary table 3), and the TG-to-DG ratio was significantly lower in sma-6(wk7), demonstrating enhanced triacylglycerol hydrolysis in these mutants. Suppressing the lipases’ activity in sma-6(wk7), by RNAi of atgl-1, lips-3, 4, 5 or 1744, facilitated fat restoration (Figure 6B-C), supporting that the active fat breakdown in BMP mutants is driven by enhanced lipolysis.

sec.title: NLP-10 and FLP-18 are starvation-induced neuropeptides
sec.p: As hypothesized in the figure 3E model, if the peripheral fat loss was triggered by dietary restriction per se, then we would expect the same neuropeptides being required in other types of diet-restricted worms, but not merely dyspepsia-induced dietary restriction. To investigate whether this neuropeptide axis was generally required in diet-restricted animals or specifically required in BMP-deficient animals, we starved wildtype and single mutants of nlp-10, flp-18, npr-35 or npr-4 before measuring fat levels. 24 hours of starvation halved intestinal lipid content in wildtype, while each single mutant maintained higher fat levels under the same starved condition (Figure 7A), phenocopying well-fed double mutants such as sma-6(wk7); nlp-10(tm6232) and so on. By qRT-PCR, we demonstrated that the expression of nlp-10, flp-18, npr-35 and npr-4 were induced in starved wildtype and starved BMP mutants (Figure 7B), suggesting that the induction of nlp-10 and flp-18 in the BMP mutants are more likely to be triggered by a general energy-insufficient status, rather than a BMP-specific regulation. In eat-4(ky5) and eat-2(ad1116), which are BMP-independent models with restricted energy intake45,46, we found that flp-18 and nlp-10, as well as several other previously screened neuropeptides that may not mediate BMP-associated fat loss (encoded by nlp-15, 21, 51 and flp-14, 27) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E), were upregulated (Figure 7C). This further supports NLP-10 and FLP-18 as general starvation-induced neuropeptides, and also verifies the findings of Harvald et al31. Collectively, although dozens of neuropeptides are transcriptionally induced by energy deficiency, only a subset of them are genetically required to stimulate fat mobilization.

sec.p: Conversely, we wondered if the mere overexpression of one component in this neuropeptide axis would be sufficient to trigger fat mobilization in well-fed wildtype. For this purpose, we generated NLP-10 overexpressed animals and NPR-4 overexpressed animals, but neither was sufficient to elicit fat loss (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B). This suggests that the neuropeptide signaling pathway is unlikely to serve as an ON/OFF switch for fat mobilization in peripheral tissues, but rather as a signal amplifier that can be modulated by the animal’s nutritional status.

In conclusion, the chronically diet-restricted status produced by either BMP-associated dyspepsia or prolonged food deprivation, could hyperactivate intestinal fat mobilization through a neuropeptide signaling axis involving the NLP-10/NPR-35 and the FLP-18/NPR-4 peptide receptor pairs. Fat loss in diet-restricted animals could be blocked by suppressing any key component — be it a peptide, a receptor, or a lipase. Given sufficient food supply, fat mobilization would require more than the overexpression of a single-factor peptide or receptor.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We demonstrate that diet-restricted C. elegans upregulates a neuropeptide signaling axis to stimulate intestinal fat mobilization. This axis involves two peptide-receptor pairs, namely NLP-10-NPR-35 and FLP-18-NPR-4, to enhance triacylglycerol hydrolysis (Figure 7D). Rather than a mutant-specific mechanism, this axis generally detects energy deficiency as an internal cue and stimulates fat breakdown as the physiological response.

Starvation-induced neuropeptide upregulation has been characterized across species. In mammals, hypothalamic NPY and AgRP expression increase upon fasting to drive hyperphagia and metabolic adaptation47,48. In fasted Drosophila, tachykinin rises to suppress lipogenesis49. C. elegans FLP-18 increases upon food deprivation to modulate food foraging behaviors50 and fat metabolism32. Our findings have traced the flp-18-secreting tissues to the npr-35-expressing cells and revealed NLP-10 in ADL neurons as an important upstream signal. The multi-functional ADL neurons have been shown to sense sex pheromones51,52 and other stimuli in the external environment, and they can also detect neuronal mitochondrial stress as an internal cue to cause physiological responses in intestine 53. In this study, we demonstrate that the ADL neurons are essential for the organism to mobilize fat in response to energy deficiency as an internal stimulus. This echoes and complements previous findings that ADL neurons regulate intestinal fat storage in response to sex pheromones in the external environment 54. Considering that the C. elegans nervous system is capable of integrating different cues (such as food abundance and pheromone concentration 55) to make behavioral decisions, the regulatory effect of ADL neurons and relevant neuropeptides on physiology and decision-making is worthy of further study. In addition to NLP-10, FLP-18, FLP-1 and FLP-4, several peptides have emerged as promising candidates for fat regulation and starvation perception, such as FLP-5, 8, 13, 24 and NLP-6, 9, 13, 35, 50 (Figure 2— figure supplement 1E). Elucidating the in vivo functions and genetic interactions of these peptides remains challenging yet critical, as such efforts would reveal the operational logic of neuropeptide signaling in modulating metabolic processes—particularly its hierarchical and additive effects on the homeostasis of lipid storage and lipolysis. While many more neuropeptide genes could be transcriptionally induced by nutrient deficit, they are dispensable for regulating fat mobilization (e.g., NLP-15, 21, 51, and FLP-14, 27, as shown in Figure 7C and (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and how these peptides differ from the fat-regulating ones in determining the organism’s metabolic set point remains interesting.

Although transcriptional induction of nlp-10 has been consistently observed in BMP mutants, eat-2/4 mutants, and fasted wildtype, the nlp-10 overexpression per se cannot trigger fat mobilization in well-fed animals with intact BMP pathway, nor can NPR-4 overexpression. This suggests that highly redundant mechanisms are programmed in neuroendocrine systems to prevent unnecessary fat mobilization, which permit the organism to store energy and substrates under nutrient-rich conditions. On the flipped side, for the diet-restricted animals to mobilize fat, a series of neuropeptides and receptors need to stay hyperactivated. Would the consistent activation of lipolysis benefit the longevity of BMP mutants? Some studies have shown that the BMP mutants are mildly long-lived 13,56. Whether the NLP-10-NPR-35-FLP-18-NPR-4 axis is involved in BMP-associated longevity would require further investigation.

In this study, the importance of including viable and fertile animals with chronic dietary restriction (i.e., BMP mutants) is self-evident for uncovering the detailed action sites and communication patterns of the NLP-10-NPR-35-FLP-18-NPR-4 axis. Now that the dyspepsia phenotype has been identified in the BMP mutants, future investigations can be designed using these chronically dietary-restricted models to address unresolved questions regarding metabolic homeostasis and physiological adaptation. Beyond its traditional bone morphogenetic roles, BMP pathway has been recognized as a multi-faced regulator in lipid metabolism with tissue specificity: In the peripheral tissues of mammals, BMP4 promotes white adipocyte differentiation and has dual roles, either promoting or repressing oxidative metabolism in a cell-context-dependent manner57,58; BMP7, in contrast, stimulates brown preadipocyte differentiation to increase energy expenditure and decrease weight gain59. In the central nervous system of mammals, BMP signaling also regulates appetite, metabolism and the whole-body energy balance60. In C. elegans, BMP pathway has been shown to interact with the insulin signaling to regulate lipid accumulation13, which is consistent to their chronically diet-restricted state. As for the precise working site of BMP signaling, pharyngeal SMA-3 has been shown to restore intestinal colonization of the pathogenic Enterobacter strain61, foreshadowing a mechanistic link between BMP signaling and bacteria processing. In wildtype, pharyngeal glands secrete mucin-like proteins to facilitate digestion62, and mucins are generally known to mediate a variety of biological processes including oral hydration and non-immune host-defense toward microbes in mammals63. Intriguingly, lacking BMP pathway upregulates most mucin-like genes (GO:1905905) 12 - whether this is an adaptation to, or a side-effect of the grinding problem merits further investigation.

In C. elegans and other models, associations between innate immune responses and BMP signaling are receiving attention 61,64–66. Lipidomic analysis of this study reveals that the levels of certain signaling lipids are very different in wildtype and sma-6(wk7). Particularly, eicosanoid, SPH, and ceramide-NP are upregulated, while LPA is downregulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), pointing to a coordinated metabolic resetting that dampens reproduction and upregulates immune responses. Specifically, LPA is a bioactive lipid mediator that facilitates germ cell survival and oocyte maturation 67,68, eicosanoids serve as CYP-dependent signaling molecules that activate innate immune responses via the p38 MAPK pathway 69, and sphingolipids like SPH and ceramide-NP reinforce intestinal epithelial barrier integrity and apical polarity 70,71. Thus, the lipidomic profile of sma-6(wk7) might reflect a systemic shift from fecundity toward stress defense. Consistently, a category of pathogen-induced genes that are BMP dependent were identified to encode lipid metabolic enzymes 14. Whether the shift from fecundity to defense happened to other types of diet-restricted worms would require further investigation.

sec.title: Resources and reagents
sec.p: C. elegans strains were cultured using nematode growth media (NGM) agar and E. coli OP50 as described 72,73, except for the RNAi experiments. For RNAi, bacteria recovered from the Ahringer RNAi library 74,75 were fed to C. elegans on NGM agar containing 1 mM of Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). All C. elegans strains were maintained at 20 °C. Supplementary table 4 describes the reagents used in this study.

Oligos used in genotyping and plasmid construction were described in Supplementary table 5. To construct plasmids, DNA fragments amplified from the genomic DNA or complementary DNA of Bristol N2 C. elegans were seamlessly cloned into the pJM23-SL2-GFP backbone. Transgenic strains were generated by standard microinjection methods 76 with 30-50 ng/μL of the corresponding plasmids and maintained by picking nematodes with transgenic markers. To verify the expression of nlp-10p::GFP, DiI staining 77 were applied with the Zeiss Axioplan2 microscopic system at the green channel (525 nm emission wavelength, 470 nm excitation wavelength) and the red channel (610 nm emission wavelength, 560 nm excitation wavelength).

sec.title: Starvation and nutrient supplementation
sec.p: To starve nematodes, synchronized L1s were cultured on NGM agar with E. coli OP50 until they reach the L4 stage, rinsed in M9 buffer, and transferred to the NGM agar without bacterial food. After 24 hours of starvation, nematodes were collected as the samples of lipid staining or qRT-PCR experiments. To supplement nematodes with extra nutrients, glucose, fructose or oleic acid was provided to culture synchronized L1s until they reach the adult stage (Day 1). Glucose or fructose were mixed into the NGM agar at 0.5% concentration (w/v). Oleic acid was mixed into the bacterial food at the ratio of 1 : 296 (v/v), and 200 μL of this mixture were provided to each φ = 6 cm NGM agar plate.

sec.title: Semi-quantification of intestinal fat levels upon fixation and lipid staining
sec.p: A Nile Red based lipid staining method, developed from Escorcia et al 78 and Stuhr et al 79, was applied to determine the relative fat levels: nematodes were briefly rinsed in M9 buffer and immediately fixed in the 1% paraformaldehyde solution for 30 min, followed by a freezing-crack step (frozen at -80 °C for no less than 2 hours) to facilitate stain permeability. Once thawed, the nematodes were rinsed by PBST buffer and 40% isopropanol solution (v/v) before they were soaked into the staining solution (1 ng/μL of Nile Red (MCE® catalog # HY-D0718) in 40% isopropanol) for 30 min. Stained nematodes were rinsed by PBST and mounted onto glass slides with 2% agarose pads, and imaged by the Zeiss Axioplan2 microscopic system at 595 nm emission wavelength and 500 nm excitation wavelength. To quantify fat levels in the intestinal region individual-by-individual, fluorescent intensities were measured by Fiji ImageJ (with the intestinal region being labelled by yellow dotted lines) 80. Mean intensity of the control group was defined as ‘1’ for normalization to calculate the relative fat levels.

sec.title: Intestinal Colony Forming Units (CFU)
sec.p: With a method developed from Portal-Celhay et al 20,81, the CFU of nematodes’ intestinal bacteria were quantified: Per each genotype, ten adults were picked onto a bacteria-free NGM agar plate containing 100 ug/mL gentamicin (to inhibit E. coli growth) to crawl freely for 5 min, and then transferred into a glass vial with M9 buffer containing 25 mM of levamisole (to pause pharyngeal pumping and defecation) and 100 μg/mL gentamicin by glass pipettes, followed by two M9 rinses; 100 μL of PBST were added to the nematode-containing vial, and each vial was manually grinded for 15 sec by a disposable rod; with PBS, the rod was rinsed and a final volume of 500 μL was achieved as the stock solution; the stock solution and its diluted solutions (101 to 105 times) were spread onto LB agar plates to score and calculate CFU per worm upon the 37°C overnight culture.

sec.title: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)
sec.p: Adult nematodes of the same genotype were collected and briefly rinsed in a 1.5mL vial with PBS solution, and 300 μL of ice-cold glutaraldehyde solution (0.67% glutaraldehyde and 0.67% Osmium in 10 mM HEPES) were added to each vial to incubate nematodes for 1 hour on ice, followed by 5 rinses of ice-cold 10 mM HEPES (15 min per each rinse). The nematodes were then fixed in ice-cold OsO4 solution (2% osmium in 10 mM HEPES) and incubated for 3 hours at 4°C. Another 5 rinses (by water) were applied before the nematodes were embedded in 2% low melt agarose and stained in 1 % uranyl acetate overnight. Upon a brief rinse in water, samples were dehydrated in a cold graded ethanol series (20 %, 50 %, 70 %, 90 %, 100 %, 100 %) for 13 min per each, followed by two acetone rinses at room temperature, and infiltrated in SPI-Pon 812 using anhydrous acetone-to-812 at different volume ratios: 3:1, 1:1, 1:3, and then 100 % of 812 overnight. Before baking at 60 °C for 48 hours, one more rinse with fresh 812 were applied. The embedded nematodes were then sectioned into 75 nm slices using the Leica UC7 ultramicrotome, stained by lead citrate for 5 min, and imaged by the Hitachi HT7800 transmission electron microscope.

sec.title: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and Gene Ontology (GO) analysis
sec.p: RNA-seq data generated in Yu et al 12 were used for the identification of DEGs and GO analysis by Metascape at https://metascape.org/ 82.

sec.title: Lipidomic profiling and data analysis
sec.p: Synchronized wildtype (Bristol N2) and sma-6(wk7) young adults (∼10,000 nematodes per genotype per replicant) were collected by M9 buffer, followed by removal of supernatant and immediate frozen via dry ice. Lipid extraction, LC-MS detection, lipid identification and quantification, and data analysis were purchased from MetwareBio Inc. To calculate the TG-to-DG ratio, corresponding area-under-curve values were summed and standardized as the dividends and divisors.

sec.title: Statistical analysis and scientific plotting
sec.p: Unless otherwise indicated, statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed Mann-Whitney test to compare two genotypes, or Kruskal-Wallis test to compare more than two genotypes. Scientific plotting was achieved by GraphPad Prism 10.1 and Adobe Illustrator 2023.

body.p: The authors study global neuropeptide changes in C. elegans mutants lacking functional BMP, using this as a viable and fertile animal model that exhibits consistent dyspepsia and chronic dietary restriction. The findings of this study are valuable as they provide a global picture of neuropeptide responses to starvation and detail a circuit from a sensory neuron to lipid metabolism in the gut. This work provides evidence that nutrient stress resulting from impaired food processing engages NLP-10-, NPR-35-, FLP-18-, and NPR-4-dependent signalling to promote fat utilization. However, the evidence is incomplete, as the order of action of the neuropeptides is weak.
Summary:

This manuscript describes how defective food grinding due to loss of TGF-beta signalling leads to fat loss via specific neuropeptides and their cognate receptors in C. elegans. They define transcriptional mechanisms from the ADL sensory neuron to neuropeptide relays from neurons to the gut, wherein enzymatic effectors mediate fat metabolism. The genetic evidence presented to support this neuropeptide circuitry is based largely on transcriptional changes detected in bulk mRNA, cell-type-specific rescue, and lipid measurements using Nile Red staining in permeabilized/fixed animals and with lipidomics. The findings are of interest to researchers in neuropeptide regulation of physiology.
Strengths:
(1) The multifaceted analysis of dbl-1 and sma-6 provides good evidence that the primary defect leading to metabolic phenotypes is due to pharyngeal function.
(2) The transcriptional survey of neuropeptide expression under fasting and in TGF-beta pathway mutants will be a useful resource for many labs studying neuropeptides in food sensing.
(3) Outlining the process from dietary restriction to fat metabolism in the gut provides a big-picture view that establishes physiological relevance.
(4) Identifying new functions for specific neuropeptides and their receptors in fat metabolism.
Weaknesses:

Evidence that links NLP-10-NPR-35 signalling to FLP-18-NPR-4 is weak, and primarily rests on overlaps in npr-35 and flp-18 expression, as well as rescue of flp-18 under the npr-35 promoter. It remains possible that FLP-18 acts from those neurons, but is not activated by NPR-35 signalling, since the mechanisms downstream of NPR-35 are unclear in this context. Strengthening this link would require showing a change in FLP-18 activity; for example, showing npr-35-dependent changes in flp-18 transcription in npr-35-expressing neurons.

The expression patterns of the neuropeptides and receptors that guide the sites of cell-specific rescue experiments are from well-fed animals. However, it remains a possibility that starvation alters neuropeptides and their receptors are expressed, which would produce a different circuit.

Different food levels produce different physiological and transcriptional responses. The manuscript largely assumes that starvation is equivalent to food reduction when they are physiologically distinct states.
Summary:

This manuscript investigates how animals adapt their metabolism to conditions of reduced nutrient availability. Using C. elegans, the authors identify a neuropeptide signaling network that promotes intestinal lipid mobilization when nutrient acquisition is compromised. The study proposes that nutrient stress activates signaling involving NLP-10, NPR-35, FLP-18, and NPR-4, ultimately leading to increased utilization of stored triglycerides.

A major strength of the work is the combination of multiple experimental approaches, including genetic analyses, neuron-specific rescue experiments, starvation paradigms, and lipid measurements. Together, these experiments support the conclusion that the identified neuropeptide pathway contributes to the regulation of energy stores during nutrient stress. The observation that similar signaling components function in both the mutant and starvation contexts strengthens the physiological relevance of the findings.
Strengths:

The revised manuscript is substantially improved and presents a coherent model linking sensory and interneuronal signaling to peripheral metabolic responses. The data convincingly establish functional roles for the identified neuropeptide components in controlling fat storage and mobilization.

Readers should keep in mind that the exact relationships among pathway components are not completely resolved. While the genetic evidence supports placement of NLP-10, NPR-35, FLP-18, and NPR-4 within a common regulatory framework, the data are somewhat less definitive regarding the precise order of signaling events and whether all interactions are direct. The authors appropriately acknowledge some of this complexity, and a clearer distinction between experimentally demonstrated versus inferred connections would further strengthen the presentation.
Overall, this is a carefully executed and biologically interesting study that advances our understanding of neuroendocrine control of metabolism during nutrient limitation.
Weaknesses:

No weaknesses were noted by this reviewer in the revision. My main comment is that whilst I appreciate the authors' efforts to refine the signaling model in response to earlier comments, the pathway architecture remains somewhat complex, particularly regarding the relationships among NLP-10, NPR-35, FLP-18, and NPR-4. I encourage the authors to make one final pass through the text and model figure to clearly distinguish interactions that are directly supported by experimental evidence from those that remain inferred based on genetic relationships. This would help readers accurately interpret the strength of evidence supporting each step of the proposed pathway.
Summary:

In this manuscript, Liu et al. used C. elegans animals lacking functional BMP as a model to dissect the neuropeptide signaling pathways that lead to BMP-associated fat loss. First, they established the BMP mutants as a model of dyspepsia that results in chronic dietary restriction. They then used this model to identify neuropeptide genes that are upregulated and required for BMP-associated fat loss. Next, they sought to identify the receptors for these neuropeptides and to place the genes in a genetic and cellular pathway. They also showed that the same neuropeptides and receptors contribute to fat loss in diet-restricted C. elegans. They conclude that they have identified a neuropeptide signaling cascade in which impaired pharyngeal function activates sensory neurons, which then signal through interneurons to enhance triglyceride hydrolysis in the intestine.
Strengths:

In this manuscript, Liu et al. characterized the pharyngeal muscles and the intestinal bacterial context of animals lacking functional BMP. They showed a correlation between BMP-associated fat loss and pharyngeal impairments that could lead to insufficient food grinding. This finding suggests that C. elegans lacking functional BMP could serve as a model for dyspepsia and chronic dietary restriction. Moreover, the authors analyzed previously published gene expression data to identify neuropeptides that are overexpressed in animals lacking BMP. They then used mutants for these neuropeptides and their receptors to determine which of these genes contribute to BMP-associated fat loss. Finally, they showed that the same neuropeptides and receptors also contribute to fat loss in diet-restricted C. elegans.
Weaknesses:

(1) The authors use double mutants between BMP pathway mutants and neuropeptide or neuropeptide receptor mutants to argue that the reduced fat levels of BMP mutants are suppressed. However, with the exception of unc-31, the fat content of the corresponding single neuropeptide or neuropeptide receptor mutant is not shown. Without these, the double-mutant phenotype cannot be interpreted as suppression, since it could reflect an independent effect on fat storage. To show that the effects are related to BMP signaling, the authors should compare wild-type animals to neuropeptide mutants in a sma-6(+) background. Similarly, the fat content of ADL-ablated animals is not shown in an otherwise wild-type background.

(2) In several places, the authors use cell-specific expression of neuropeptides to conclude that a given neuropeptide acts in a particular cell type (e.g., Figure 4B,C; Figure 5C,D). However, because neuropeptides are secreted and can act at a distance, expression in a non-native cell type may rescue the phenotype. These experiments therefore show sufficiency but do not establish the endogenous site of action. Cell-specific knockout or knockdown, or expression from control promoters in unrelated cell types, would help address this.

(3) The authors report that expressing npr-35 from two promoters with non-overlapping expression each fully restores the low-fat phenotype of sma-6; npr-35 mutants. This is surprising for a receptor and is difficult to interpret.

(4) The authors identify neuropeptide genes co-expressed with npr-35 and follow up on flp-18. The rationale for restricting the search to co-expressed neuropeptides may bias hypothesis generation. Similarly, the authors show that flp-1 and flp-4, in addition to flp-18, contribute to BMP-associated fat loss, but only flp-18 is examined further because of its overlapping co-expression with npr-35, again creating a bias in the investigation of the role of neuropeptide signaling in BMP-associated fat loss.

(5) It is difficult to interpret the experiment in Figure 5E, where the authors conclude that npr-4 is required in flp-18-overexpressing animals. Without a demonstrated fat-loss phenotype from overexpressing flp-18, a requirement for npr-4 in those animals cannot be meaningfully assessed.

Overall, the authors convincingly identify neuropeptides and receptors that are overexpressed and that contribute to fat loss. However, several points make it difficult to fully support the proposed model and the linear pathway from the pharynx to the intestine through ADL sensory neurons and interneurons. These include the absence of phenotypic analysis of the single mutants, the challenges of interpreting cell-specific rescue experiments when studying neuropeptide function, the fact that additional neuropeptides causing BMP-associated fat loss are identified but not studied further, and results that do not necessarily point to a linear pathway (e.g., the triple mutant sma-6; nlp-10; npr-35 has a stronger phenotype than the double mutants with sma-6, the fat loss caused by overexpression of nlp-10 in a sma-6 background is not suppressed by npr-35, and the flp-18 overexpression experiment is difficult to interpret). The reviewer therefore suggests that the linearity of this pathway, and the sites of action of the neuropeptides and receptors, should be presented more cautiously or supported by additional data.

body.p: We thank Reviewing Editor, Senior Editor and the three reviewers for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that the reviewers regard the central finding that impaired pharyngeal function engages neuropeptide signaling to modify intestinal lipid metabolism as physiologically meaningful and supported by multiple lines of evidence. At the same time, we recognize that the reviews converge on a central concern: the evidence for the order of neuropeptides’ action is weak. The reviewers also suggest us to distinguish more clearly between what our experiments demonstrate and what we infer, to present the pathway as less strictly linear, and to be more explicit about the limits of cell-specific rescue for secreted peptides. We take these points seriously, and we are exploring possible revisions in light of them.

At present, this rests mainly on two observations: the overlap between npr-35 and flp-18 expression reported in public databases, and the ability of npr-35p::FLP-18 (or ttx-3p::FLP-18) to restore fat levels. To test this directly, we will begin by measuring flp-18 transcript levels in two comparisons: (1) well-fed npr-35(lf) versus well-fed sma-6(lf); npr-35(lf), and (2) well-fed npr-35(lf) versus fasted npr-35(lf). In addition, transcriptional levels of nlp-10, flp-1, and flp-4 can be compared in these worms. If NPR-35 activity is required for flp-18 induction when nutrients are limiting, removing npr-35 should blunt or reduce this induction in the sma-6-mutated or nutrient-deprived backgrounds; If NPR-35 activity is not required, flp-18 induction should not be affected. A third possibility is that NPR-35 amplifies FLP-18 signaling, which would not conflict with the nutrient-sensing role of FLP-18 per se. Regardless of the outcome, we will rewrite this section to clarify the step from NLP-10 to FLP-18.

body.p: This is a fair point, and we accept it as a limitation of the present study. The expression patterns that guided our rescue experiments were defined in well-fed animals, using published datasets (Beets et al., 2023; Ripoll-Sánchez et al., 2023; Ghaddar et al., 2023) and our own transcriptional reporters under well-fed conditions. We cannot exclude that nutrient status alters the expression of these peptides and receptors.

We plan to examine intestinal npr-4p::GFP in well-fed and starved animals in the near future. We could also attempt to image neuronal npr-35p::GFP, but this would be technically challenging given mosaic expression and issues with worm orientation. In the Discussion of future versions, we will state this caveat and will be careful to describe our rescue experiments as identifying the cells in which a gene is sufficient to support the phenotype under the conditions tested, rather than as confirming the circuit in the starved animals.

disp-quote.p: Different food levels produce different physiological and transcriptional responses. The manuscript largely assumes that starvation is equivalent to food reduction when they are physiologically distinct states.

body.p: We agree, and we regret that our wording implied equivalence. Our intention was not to treat all nutrient-limited states as identical but to ask whether a common pathway is engaged. The observation that the same components are required under each of these energy-deficient conditions supports the physiological relevance of the pathway. We will rewrite the relevant sentences to convey this intent and to avoid implying that different nutritional states are equivalent. We acknowledge the limitation that our design cannot determine the degree of energy deficit required to engage the neuropeptides, or whether the response is graded across milder and more severe restriction.

body.p: We agree with the underlying point of this criticism. Expression of a secreted peptide from a heterologous promoter demonstrates that the peptide can act when produced in that cell; however, it does not establish where the peptide acts under physiological conditions. We are grateful to the reviewer for these suggestions and have carefully considered both approaches. While we fully appreciate their potential value, we believe it is more appropriate to regard them as complementary rather than decisive, and we would like to explain our reasoning in detail.

The first approach, cell-specific knockdown, may or may not affect peripheral lipid catabolism in this system, because (1) the number of peptides capable of influencing fat storage is large, as shown in Figure 2 – figure supplement 1D, E, and (2) the expression pattern of a receptor or peptide gene may be altered under nutrient-deprived conditions (as in comments of R1). The axis we describe could be buffered by ligand redundancy, as our data on FLP-1 and FLP-4 show. Under such redundancy, a negative result from knocking down a single peptide in a group of cells would not exclude a physiological role for that peptide in that cell. The second approach, expression from a control promoter in an unrelated cell, might also be complicated by the point that R1 raises: if nutrient status alters the expression of peptides and their receptors, it becomes difficult to specify a cell type that is reliably “unrelated” to lipid regulation in the relevant physiological state. Therefore, we will modify our manuscript to describe the rescue experiments consistently as demonstrating sufficiency and discuss this limitation frankly.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this point, and we realize that our description was not sufficiently precise. The two promoters drive expression in different subsets of npr-35-expressing neurons; however, in both cases npr-35 is overexpressed, as is typical of C. elegans transgenic lines. A non-exclusive explanation also seems plausible to us: the two cell populations (nmr-1-positive & ttx-3-positive) may converge on a shared downstream output, which is the release of FLP-18 from these interneurons, so that restoring receptor function in either population restores the ultimate output. We will revise the text to present both possibilities and to describe the result in terms of sufficiency.

body.p: We accept that restricting our attention to peptides co-expressed with npr-35 introduced a bias, and we will state this openly. We would like to note two considerations that may help contextualize this bias. First, flp-18 showed the strongest transcriptional induction among the peptides we examined (Figure 2 - figure supplement 1D), and this was an important reason for prioritizing it. Second, our subsequent analysis was not confined to co-expressed peptides: flp-1 and flp-4 are also required for BMP-associated fat loss, while flp-1 shows little overlap with npr-35 and does not appear to be released from npr-35-expressing neurons (Figure 5 - figure supplement 1D). The co-expression therefore served as an entry point rather than as a filter. We will clearly describe this rationale in the text, present the broader set of candidate peptides identified in our screen, and note that additional peptides are likely to contribute to fat regulation. We hope that the dataset will support work in this direction, both in our laboratory and in other laboratories.

disp-quote.p: (5) It is difficult to interpret the experiment in Figure 5E, where the authors conclude that npr-4 is required in flp-18-overexpressing animals. Without a demonstrated fat-loss phenotype from overexpressing flp-18, a requirement for npr-4 in those animals cannot be meaningfully assessed.

body.p: We assume that the reviewer is referring to Figure 5G, and we apologize for the confusion in this panel. This confusion may have arisen from the way we arranged the columns. The experiment was designed to ask whether npr-4 is required for overdosed FLP-18 to function (with overexpression ensured by sma-6(lf)-induced upregulation and the ttx-3p::FLP-18 transgene). Therefore, a clearer way to organize these columns would be to swap the third and fourth columns, which we will do in the revised version.

We nonetheless agree with the reviewer’s underlying point. Because ttx-3p::FLP-18 alone does not reduce fat in the already fat-deficient sma-6(lf), the assay has limited dynamic range. So, a requirement for npr-4 cannot be established from this comparison alone. We will reorder the columns, correct the legend, and present the panel as consistent with npr-4 acting downstream of flp-18. We would also place greater emphasis on the comparisons in Figure 5B, in which sma-6(lf); npr-4(lf) retained more fat than sma-6(lf); flp-18(lf), an outcome expected if the receptor acts downstream of the ligand and if additional ligands converge on NPR-4.

disp-quote.p: Overall, the authors convincingly identify neuropeptides and receptors that are overexpressed and that contribute to fat loss. However, several points make it difficult to fully support the proposed model and the linear pathway from the pharynx to the intestine through ADL sensory neurons and interneurons. These include the absence of phenotypic analysis of the single mutants, the challenges of interpreting cell-specific rescue experiments when studying neuropeptide function, the fact that additional neuropeptides causing BMP-associated fat loss are identified but not studied further, and results that do not necessarily point to a linear pathway (e.g., the triple mutant sma-6; nlp-10; npr-35 has a stronger phenotype than the double mutants with sma-6, the fat loss caused by overexpression of nlp-10 in a sma-6 background is not suppressed by npr-35, and the flp-18 overexpression experiment is difficult to interpret). The reviewer therefore suggests that the linearity of this pathway, and the sites of action of the neuropeptides and receptors, should be presented more cautiously or supported by additional data.

body.p: We are grateful for this synthesis, which we take as the central conceptual comment of the review. We agree that our data do not support a strictly linear pathway, and we will revise both the text and the model figure accordingly.

The two observations the reviewer cites, that the triple mutant sma-6; nlp-10; npr-35 retains more fat than either double mutant, and that removing npr-35 does not offset the fat loss caused by NLP-10 overexpression, point in the same direction: NLP-10 likely acts through receptor(s) in addition to NPR-35. We consider this plausible on independent grounds. Because nlp-10 is induced when nutrients are limiting, an additional receptor might be engaged only when NLP-10 rises above its basal level, or only when the nlp-10 expression domain expands under dietary restriction. Either scenario would explain why such a receptor has not emerged from interaction screens carried out under standard feeding conditions.

In the revision, we will describe the axis as a genetic framework in which the NLP-10/NPR-35 and FLP-18/NPR-4 modules are related, with branch points at both the ligand and receptor levels, and we will mark the connections that remain inferential. We will also note that the conservation of NPR-35 across nematodes (Beets et al., 2023; Golinelli et al., 2024) may provide an entry point for identifying additional NLP-10 receptors, and we would welcome works in that direction.

disp-quote.p: The manuscript could provide more nuanced and accurate context in several areas:

(1) Work from the Ashrafi Lab (Greer et al., 2008, Cunningham et al., 2014) has described roles for daf-7 (another TGF-beta) in fat metabolism and should be cited to provide a more comprehensive introduction.

body.p: Thanks! We will cite the work from the Ashrafi laboratory on the DAF-7 branch of TGF-β signaling and on fat metabolism in the Introduction of the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) The interpretation of the unc-31 phenotype is not as straightforward as the text indicates. unc-31 does not only affect DCVs, unc-31 mutants also have SV defects. Moreover, DCVs also release TGF-beta and monoamines. Thus, an unc-31 phenotypes does not necessarily implicate neuropeptides.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this comment and apologize for the confusion. In fact, in addition to analyzing unc-31(lf); sma-2(lf), we analyzed the fat levels of egl-3(lf); sma-2(lf) and egl-21(lf); sma-2(lf), and the phenotypes caused by the loss of egl-3 or egl-21 were similar to those caused by unc-31(lf) in these BMP mutants. We omitted these data from the previous version for simplicity, and we acknowledge that we wrongly overlooked the non-DSV roles of UNC-31/CAPS. We will revise this section by adding additional data on egl-3 and egl-21.

disp-quote.p: (3) In lines 132-134, the logic of the argument is not clear, since it does not indicate how sma-3 rescue in the pharynx is linked to sma-6 in the ADL neurons.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer’s comment and will remove the wording related to sma-3 rescue from this sentence in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (4) Lines 271-273 indicate that BMP mutants are mildly long-lived. This point is only partially correct. Depending on the food level, daf-7 mutants can be long-lived, have no phenotype, or be short-lived.

body.p: Thank you. We will rewrite the section on lifespan so that it reflects the lifespan of daf-7 mutants and BMP mutants properly.

disp-quote.p: This manuscript could also be improved by clarifying or acknowledging several technical gaps/weaknesses:
(1) For Supplemental Figure 2d, it is not clear if there is any correction for multiple hypothesis testing when assaying multiple neuropeptides. This point should be clarified.

body.p: We acknowledge that we did not perform any multiple hypothesis testing on the data shown in this figure panel in the previous version. Due to technical limitations, we were unable to compare all qRT-PCR groups within a single 96-well plate. The qRT-PCR assays were performed separately for each gene, with double mutant and single mutant worms collected in the same-day manner. Accordingly, these qRT-PCR results are not suitable for comparisons between different genes, but they do allow valid comparisons between the double mutant and the corresponding single mutant within the same target gene. We will clarify this point in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) Strains used in this work have only been outcrossed twice, which leaves 25% of mutations. The parent strains with tm and ok alleles were isolated after mutagenesis and are expected to contain thousands of mutations. Two outcrosses imply that several hundred unlinked mutations remain, which weakens the genetic evidence.

body.p: Because most of the data were obtained from double mutants (e.g., sma-6(lf); nlp-10(lf), sma-6(lf); npr-35(lf)), we performed at least one additional round of outcrossing by introducing the single mutants into the BMP mutants. We therefore expect that the background mutation load in these double mutants is lower than 25%. As we plan to do more experiments on the single mutants, we will first increase the number of outcrosses before measuring fat levels.

disp-quote.p: (3) More details are needed on the methods related to fluorescence microscopy, especially since most of the manuscript's conclusions rest on quantitative fluorescence. It is important to describe the light source and whether there was any calibration to control for variable fluorescence due to the equipment.

body.p: Thank you. We will do so. All Nile Red imaging was performed on the same microscopic system, which is not a confocal microscope but an upright widefield microscope, which captures the full depth of field along the z-axis (rather than a single optical section). In the revised manuscript, we will expand the fluorescence microscopy methods to describe the illumination source, the acquisition settings, and the measures taken, etc.

disp-quote.p: Minor Comments

(1) The finding that NLP-10 overexpression alone does not produce a strong phenotype in wild-type animals is intriguing. A brief discussion of how this observation fits into the proposed model would be useful for readers.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer that NLP-10 overexpression alone does not produce a strong phenotype in wild-type animals, which is intriguing. We have not yet performed a detailed mechanistic analysis of this phenomenon. We speculate that animals likely possess metabolic homeostatic mechanisms that buffer against perturbations in NLP-10 levels. As R1 suggested, it is also possible that dietary restriction or starvation conditions may broaden the expression range of nlp-10 or its receptor(s). We will discuss this possibility and its relationship to our proposed model in greater depth in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) Some figure legends describing complex genetic comparisons could benefit from additional explanatory language highlighting the key conclusion from each experiment. This would improve accessibility of the paper.

body.p: Figure legends will be improved in the revised version.

disp-quote.p: Overall Recommendation:
The manuscript has been substantially strengthened through revision, and the remaining issues are largely matters of clarity and presentation. I am supportive of the paper following minor revision.

body.p: Thank you again for your feedback. Revisions will include updated data and improved wording in future versions.

disp-quote.p: (1) dbl-1 mutants are mentioned in the Introduction without explanation. The authors should briefly describe what dbl-1 encodes and how it relates to the BMP pathway studied here.

body.p: We apologize for this confusion and will introduce DBL-1 properly in the Introduction by identifying it as the C. elegans BMP ligand that signals through the SMA-6/SMA-2/SMA-3/SMA-4 pathway.

disp-quote.p: (2) Lines 19, 60, and 238: It is unclear what exactly the authors mean by "mutant-specific effects," "mutant-specific phenomenon," and "mutant-specific mechanism."

body.p: We will replace the term “mutant-specific” with alternative wording. By this term, we meant “specific to BMP mutants”, as opposed to a general response to nutrient insufficiency.

disp-quote.p: (3) Lines: 56-57 The authors state that "the ADL sensory neurons release neuropeptide NLP-10... to promote the secretion of... FLP18". To make this statement, the authors need to use a neuropeptide secretion assay (e.g., the coelomocyte release assay) to show their claim or tone down the language.

body.p: We will tone down the language since we do not measure peptide secretion directly.

disp-quote.p: (4) ADL ablation in the sma-6; nlp-10 double mutant could help support the authors' hypothesis.

body.p: We agree that ADL ablation in sma-6(lf); nlp-10(lf) could in principle provide additional information. However, we do not consider this experiment essential for the revised manuscript. Our main concern is that metabolic regulation is mediated by many peptides with partially redundant and compensatory functions. Therefore, the outcome of ADL ablation in sma-6(lf); nlp-10(lf) would be difficult to interpret unambiguously. We will acknowledge this limitation in the Discussion of the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (5) Figure 3D: The authors perform an ADL-specific rescue experiment to show that expression of sma-6 in ADL does not rescue the fat content defect of sma-6 mutants. Because this is a negative result, it is hard to interpret unless the authors first show that the construct is indeed expressed in ADL (e.g., by co-expressing a fluorescent reporter from the same transcript, such as in an operon with sma-6) and, second, that they can rescue the sma-6 phenotype by expression in the pharynx, especially if they want to support the model shown in Figure 3E.

body.p: We will either image ADL neurons expressing srh-220p::sma-6::sl2::gfp, using DiI filling as an ADL landmark, or test whether pharyngeal expression of SMA-6 rescues the phenotype.

disp-quote.p: (6) Figure 5G: the figure legend describes a different experiment than the one shown in the figure.

body.p: We will correct the legend for Figure 5G.

disp-quote.p: Minor points:
(1) Line 106: change "verify" to "verified".
(2) Line 134: change "might have worked" to "might work".
(3) Line 148: replace the ";" at the end of the phrase with a full stop.
(4) Figure 5- figure supplement 1E: the title reads "npr-4 is required in flp-10 overexpressed animals". The authors presumably mean "nlp-10-overexpressing animals".

body.p: We thank the reviewer for pointing out these flaws and will make corrections in subsequent versions.
